name: Mandarin Chinese written in Pinyin
variety: Standard Chinese (Putonghua), Beijing-based pronunciation; the same spoken language and the same sounds as cmn, written in Hanyu Pinyin instead of Han characters
sources: Lee, Wai-Sum & Zee, Eric (2003). Standard Chinese (Beijing). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 33(1), 109-112.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, citation monosyllables
vowel_formants.source: Wu Zongji 1986 (table reproduced in Lin & Wang 1992)
vowel_formants.notes: Same data as cmn. F1 of /a/ (1000 Hz) is higher than later studies of male speakers usually report, so treat it as an upper bound.

contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated in every stop and affricate; Pinyin writes the unaspirated series b d g z zh j and the aspirated series p t k c ch q, and neither series is voiced
three sibilant places: dental (z c s), retroflex (zh ch sh, with r) and alveolo-palatal (j q x)
four lexical tones plus a toneless (neutral) syllable type
alveolar versus velar nasal coda (n, ng)
front rounded y (Pinyin ü, written u after j q x y) against i and u
plain versus rhotacised rhymes (erhua, written with a final r)
allophony: Pinyin i stands for three sounds: [i] in general, the syllabic dental approximant [ɹ̩] after z c s, and the syllabic retroflex approximant [ɻ̩] after zh ch sh r
Pinyin u after j q x y is [y]; Pinyin e is [ɤ] in an open syllable, [e] in ei and after i or ü (ie, üe are [jɛ], [ɥɛ]), [ə] before n and ng
Pinyin a is [a] in open syllables and before i and n, [ɑ] before o (ao) and ng, and [ɛ] in ian and üan
Pinyin o after b p m f is [wo]; ong is [ʊŋ]; iu, ui and un are abbreviations of [jou], [wei] and [wən]
the alveolo-palatals j q x occur only before i and ü, where the dental, retroflex and velar series never occur
Pinyin r is an approximant [ɻ] with weak frication at most; Pinyin h varies from velar [x] to uvular [χ] or glottal [h]
coda n and ng are often realised as nasalisation of the vowel with incomplete oral closure
unaspirated stops and affricates may be voiced between vowels in neutral-tone syllables
syllables written with an initial vowel may begin with a glottal stop or a weak fricative (zero initial); the apostrophe of Pinyin (Xi'an) marks such a syllable boundary
syllable_structure: (C)(G)V(X) plus tone, where G is j, w or ɥ and X is n, ŋ or an offglide i or u; ɚ and erhua rhymes add a rhotic coda
phonotactics: no consonant clusters; the only codas are n and ŋ (and the rhotic of erhua)
no final stops and no final m
labials combine with w only before o (bo, po, mo, fo); f does not precede i or y
apical vowels only after the dental and retroflex sibilants; alveolo-palatals only before high front vowels and glides
erhua merges the suffix -r with the rhyme: codas n and i are dropped, a velar nasal coda leaves nasalisation on the rhotacised vowel
every full syllable is heavy; neutral-tone syllables are light

stress.type: no contrastive word stress; full-toned (heavy) versus neutral-tone (light) syllables
stress.rule: Every full-toned syllable is prominent and neutral-tone syllables are weak; in a word of two full syllables the last is usually slightly longer in citation (Chao 1968), though Duanmu (2007) analyses words as trochaic.
stress.cues: duration and expansion of the tonal pitch range; intensity is secondary; vowel quality reduces only in neutral-tone syllables

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate, only in neutral-tone syllables: vowels centralise, diphthongs simplify, codas weaken

length.notes: No length contrast. The vowel of an open full syllable is long, vowels before a coda are short; neutral-tone syllables are about half to 60 percent as long as full syllables (Lin & Yan 1980).

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Chao & Chen 2008; Rochet & Fei 1991 report longer aspirated values, near 100 ms, in isolated words

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; gradual declination across the phrase, lowering of high targets after a low tone, and extra lowering of the final syllable
intonation.yes_no_question: with the particle ma (neutral tone) or without it, the pitch register of the whole sentence is raised and declination is reduced, with the largest rise on the last syllables; the final tone keeps its shape but is higher and ends higher (Shen 1990; Liu & Xu 2005)
intonation.wh_question: the wh-word is focused: its tones have an expanded pitch range, and the range after it is compressed and lowered
intonation.continuation: non-final phrases end without final lowering, followed by pitch reset at the start of the next phrase; final syllable lengthened
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; focus expands the pitch range of the tones on the focused word and compresses the range of everything after it (Xu 1999)
intonation.notes: Intonation is carried by register and range changes laid over the tones, not by replacing them.

inventory.name: tone 1, yīnpíng, high level; Pinyin macron (mā) or digit 1
inventory.description: High level. After a lower tone it starts below its target and reaches the high level during the first half of the syllable.
inventory.connected_speech: 55; onset pulled toward the end of the preceding tone; slightly lower late in a phrase through declination

inventory.name: tone 2, yángpíng, high rising; Pinyin acute (má) or digit 2
inventory.description: Mid to high rise. The first third of the syllable is level or falls slightly; the rise is concentrated in the later part and the peak is reached at or just after the end of the syllable.
inventory.connected_speech: 35, often 24 to 34 in running speech; between a tone 1 or tone 2 and another full tone it may flatten toward high level at fast rates (Chao 1968)
inventory.duration: long, second longest in citation form

inventory.name: tone 3, shǎngshēng, low (dipping); Pinyin caron (mǎ) or digit 3
inventory.description: Low falling then rising in isolation and before a pause. The essential target is low; the final rise belongs to the pre-pausal form.
inventory.connected_speech: 21 (half third) before tones 1, 2, 4 and before most neutral-tone syllables; 35 before another tone 3; 214 only before a pause, in isolation or under emphasis
inventory.phonation: modal, very often creaky at the low point
inventory.duration: longest in citation form (214); short as the half third (21)

inventory.name: tone 4, qùshēng, high falling; Pinyin grave (mà) or digit 4
inventory.description: Fall from the top to the bottom of the range; the peak comes shortly after the start of the syllable, not at its very onset.
inventory.connected_speech: 53 (half fourth) before another tone 4; in non-final position the fall often stops short of the floor (52 or 53)
inventory.phonation: modal, may end in creak at the bottom of the range

inventory.name: neutral tone, qīngshēng; unmarked in Pinyin, digit 5 (sometimes 0) in numbered Pinyin
inventory.description: Toneless weak syllable with no citation form. Its pitch is set by the preceding tone: half-low after tone 1, mid after tone 2, half-high after tone 3, low after tone 4 (Chao 1968).
inventory.connected_speech: a weak mid target approached slowly, so that in a run of neutral-tone syllables pitch drifts from the end of the last full tone toward mid-low over several syllables (Chen & Xu 2006)
inventory.phonation: modal, often lax with low intensity
inventory.duration: short, about half to 60 percent of a full syllable

sandhi: Pinyin spelling writes the citation tone; none of the changes below is shown in the spelling (nǐ hǎo, yī gè and bù shì are written so but said ní hǎo, yí ge and bú shì), so a reader must apply them
third-tone sandhi: tone 3 becomes a rising tone (35) before another tone 3
half third: tone 3 is low falling 21 without the final rise before tones 1, 2, 4 and before most neutral-tone syllables; the full 214 appears only before a pause, in isolation or under emphasis

in runs of three or more third tones the rule follows prosodic grouping: left-branching [[A B] C] gives 35 35 214, right-branching [A [B C]] gives 21 35 214, with 35 35 214 also possible at fast rates (Shih 1997; Chen 2000; Duanmu 2007)

一 yī: tone 1 in isolation, in counting, in ordinals and at the end of a word; tone 4 (yì) before tones 1, 2 and 3; tone 2 (yí) before tone 4 and before neutral-tone ge; neutral between reduplicated verbs
不 bù: tone 4, but tone 2 (bú) before another tone 4; neutral in A-not-A forms and potential complements
tone 4 before tone 4 is a half fall 53; the second keeps 51 (Chao 1968)
neutral tone: pitch depends on the preceding tone, 2 after tone 1, 3 after tone 2, 4 after tone 3, 1 after tone 4
tone.neutral_tone: Short, weak, toneless syllable, written without a tone mark. Pitch after tone 1 about 2, after tone 2 about 3, after tone 3 about 4, after tone 4 about 1. Duration about half to 60 percent of a full syllable, lower intensity, centralised vowel, weakened coda.
tone.notes: See cmn for the findings of Xu (1997, 1999) and Chen & Xu (2006); they apply unchanged, since this is the same spoken language.

phonation: creaky voice is frequent at the low point of tone 3 and at the end of tone 4 (Kuang 2017)
no phonation contrast in consonants; stops and affricates contrast in aspiration only

problems: only Pinyin with tone digits is read reliably (ni3 hao3); standard Pinyin with tone marks is handled by replacing the accented vowel with vowel plus digit in place, which works only when the marked vowel is the last letter of the syllable (mā, nǐ) and fails otherwise (hǎo becomes ha3o, zhōngguó likewise) and the word is then spelled out in English
a syllable with no tone digit is read as an English word (ma is said as English), so the neutral tone must be written with the digit 5
ü with a tone digit is read as English (nü3, lü4); only the substitute spelling with v works (nv3, lv4)
jiong, qiong and xiong are read as English because the final iong is missing from letter group L03 in cmn_rules
erhua spellings (hua1r5, huar1) are read as English

the tone changes of 一 and 不 are not applied to Pinyin input, because they exist only as Han-character word pairs in dictsource/extra/cmn_listx: yi1 ge4 and bu4 shi4 are spoken with their citation tones
third-tone sandhi is applied to every adjacent pair regardless of prosodic grouping (xiao3 lao3 hu3 is 35 35 214 instead of 21 35 214)
no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c ignores the clause type, and a question gives the same audio as a statement
the tonal pitch range is under 5 semitones (about 75 to 99 Hz with the voice setting 'pitch 80 118', measured on the output)
no tonal coarticulation, a short pause between words ('words 1'), no creaky phonation on tone 3, no vowel reduction in the neutral tone
tone 4 before tone 4 becomes 53 only inside one written word; in Pinyin typed with spaces between syllables the rule never applies
good: third-tone sandhi (35 before another third tone, 21 before other tones, 214 before a pause) and the neutral-tone heights 22, 33, 44, 11 are computed in C, in CalcPitches_Tone(), so they also apply to Pinyin input and across spaces
aspirated and unaspirated stops and affricates, the three sibilant series and both apical vowels are present
the three values of Pinyin i and the [y] value of u after j q x y are chosen correctly by the rules

notes: The voice file sit/cmn-Latn-pinyin has the same settings as sit/cmn (phonemes cmn, dictionary cmn, words 1, pitch 80 118, dict_min 100000); the two voices behave identically and both also read Han characters. As in other Latin-script voices, a full stop ends the sentence only when the next word begins with a capital letter; otherwise the clause continues and a final third tone is said as 21.
